column1: # title: ENG-205 Midterm — 1 Middle Ages Intro

column2: From the Latin medium (middle) and aevum (age), so it means the "middle age" between the fall of Rome and the Renaissance.

column1: 02. Span of the Middle Ages in English literature
column2: From the collapse of Roman rule in Britain (about 450) to the start of the Renaissance (about 1485).

column1: 03. Why Britain was open to invaders
column2: The Romans withdrew from Britain around 407-410, leaving a native Celtic population ill-prepared to defend itself.

column1: 04. Who settled England after the Romans left
column2: The Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, Germanic tribes who came as mercenaries and set up their own kingdoms.
Old English, a Germanic language, rather than the Celtic of the natives or the Latin of the Romans.

column1: 06. The three language periods the Norton describes, in order
column2: First Old English (Anglo-Saxon), then Anglo-Norman French after the Norman Conquest of 1066, then Middle English, which displaced French by the end of the 1300s.
Early Modern English, the language of Shakespeare, which grew into the English we speak now.
William the Conqueror's French-speaking Normans took England, so French ruled for about two centuries and poured thousands of French words into English.
The simplified, French-mixed English that re-emerged after the Conquest, the language of Chaucer and of Sir Gawain.
It relies on alliteration (repeated first consonant sounds) and a strong pause, the caesura, in the middle of each line, and it does not rhyme.

column1: 11. How Chaucer's Middle English poetry sounds
column2: It uses rhymed couplets, pairs of lines that rhyme, with five stresses per line (iambic pentameter).
A strong pause in the middle of a line of poetry, splitting each Old English line into two half-lines.
Repetition of the same first consonant sound in nearby words, the backbone of Old English verse.
A compound metaphor used in Old English poetry for a simple noun, like "whale-road" for the sea.

column1: 15. How to spot Old English on a test
column2: Strange letters like þ and æ, words such as "Hwæt," and a text that is unreadable to a modern reader.

column1: 16. How to spot Middle English on a test
column2: Readable but odd spellings with final -e's and words like "quod she," "eek," and "sith," usually in rhymed couplets (Chaucer).
